## Table 1 — the field tower, as Bitcoin Script

Every module below is proven against `bsv.Script.Interpreter` under relay
policy flags at the BLS12-381 prime.

Two columns, because a module has two honest sizes and neither is *the* size.

**Standalone** is the module alone: it pushes the 381-bit prime itself, 49
bytes, which a locking script has to do once however many operations follow.

**Marginal** is the same module with the prime already supplied as a stack
value. For the small modules that is much smaller — `fp2.mul` is 39 rather
than 90, a difference larger than the module. For the large ones it is slightly
*larger*, and the reason is worth stating: a prime pushed by the module's own
prologue sits directly above its inputs, while one supplied beneath twenty-four
of them is deeper, and an `OP_PICK` past index 16 costs a byte more. Neither
column is a lower bound on the other; the depth of a constant is part of its
cost.

| module | operation | standalone | marginal | opcodes |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `fp2.mul` | Karatsuba, three Fp multiplications | 90 | 39 | 30 |
| `fp2.sqr` | two Fp multiplications | 77 | 22 | 22 |
| `fp2.add` | | 64 | 13 | 14 |
| `fp2.sub` | | 68 | 18 | 18 |
| `fp2.neg` | | 63 | 14 | 14 |
| `fp2.conj` | the Fp2 Frobenius, p ≡ 3 (mod 4) | 59 | 9 | 10 |
| `fp2.mulXi` | multiply by ξ = u + 1, no multiplications | 67 | 15 | 16 |
| `fp2.inv` | **witnessed**: a·a⁻¹ = 1, both bounds | 101 | 51 | 36 |
| `fp6.mul` | Karatsuba, six Fp2 multiplications | 756 | 721 | 520 |
| `fp12.mul` | Karatsuba, eighteen Fp2 multiplications | 3,073 | 3,110 | 2,036 |
| `fp12.sqr` | general squaring | 2,292 | 2,301 | 1,540 |
| `fp12.cycSqr` | Granger–Scott, cyclotomic subgroup only | 1,259 | 1,292 | 968 |
| `fp12.mulLine` | sparse: nine of twelve coefficients are zero | 2,051 | 2,018 | 1,310 |
| `fp12.frob` | f ↦ f^p, six conjugations and seven products | 715 | 675 | 330 |
| `fp12.inv` | **witnessed**: one Fp12 product and twelve bounds | 3,431 | 3,414 | 2,166 |
| `fp12.powX` | f ↦ f^\|x\|, MSB-first, 63 squarings and 5 products | 98,902 | 101,353 | 71,954 |
| `g2.stepDouble` | tangent at T, and 2T | 552 | 503 | 375 |
| `g2.stepAdd` | chord through T and Q, and T + Q | 535 | 487 | 363 |
| `g1.onCurve` | y² = x³ + 4 | 72 | 21 | 17 |
| `g2.onCurve` | y² = x³ + 4(u + 1) | 178 | 127 | 102 |
| `g1.inSubgroup` | **witnessed**: the curve, and φ(P) = [−x²]P by two ladders | 8,517 | 9,321 | 6,032 |
| `g2.inSubgroup` | the twist, and T = −ψ(Q) for the loop's T = [\|x\|]Q | 389 | 340 | 144 |

**Cyclotomic squaring is 43.9% smaller than general squaring**, and the sparse line
product is 35.1% smaller than a general Fp12 product.

## Table 2 — the pairing

| stage | composition | bytes | opcodes | witnessed values |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Miller loop | 63 tangents, 5 chords, 68 line products, 63 squarings | 332,977 | 215,308 | 136 |
| final exponentiation | easy part, 5 ladders, 15 terms, 19 Frobenius maps | 473,466 | 323,175 | 72 |
| **e(P, Q)** | the two, chained | **817,031** | **538,743** | **208** |

The stages do not sum to the whole: chaining them costs
10,588 bytes that neither separate measurement contains.

## Table 3 — products of pairings share the accumulator

The squaring belongs to the *bit*, not to the line, so k pairings on one Miller
accumulator pay for 63 squarings between them and one final exponentiation.

| pairings | as a product | as separate pairings | saved |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 817,031 | 817,031 | — |
| 2 | 1,024,268 | 1,634,062 | 609,794 |
| 3 | 1,227,915 | 2,451,093 | 1,223,178 |

Each pairing after the first costs about 203,647 bytes rather than 817,031.

## Table 4 — a Groth16 verifier

e(A, B) · e(−L, γ) · e(−C, δ) = e(α, β), with 2 public inputs fixed at lock time.

| | |
| --- | ---: |
| locking script | 1,246,986 bytes |
| opcodes | 786,448 |
| witnessed values | 752 |
| chosen by the spender | Ax, Ay, Bx0, Bx1, By0, By1, Cx, Cy |
| chosen by the locking script | γ, δ, L, and e(α, β) |
| subgroup checks, A, C ∈ G1 and B ∈ G2 | 17,790 bytes, 1.4% |
| the same verifier without them | 1,229,196 bytes |

The row naming what the locking script chooses is the soundness property. A
spender who could choose γ could choose one satisfying the equation for a proof
of nothing. The subgroup rows are the other half of it: a point outside its
subgroup is still a point, and the pairing is not bilinear on it.

## Table 5 — what the network has executed

| | bytes | share of a pairing | status |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Miller loop, complete | 332,977 | 40.8% | **mainnet** |
| final exponentiation, complete | 473,466 | 57.9% | **mainnet** |
| e(P, Q) in one script | 817,031 | 100% | interpreter |
| `fp12.powX`, superseded | 98,902 | — | mainnet |

**A complete BLS12-381 pairing has been evaluated by the Bitcoin network**, as
two inputs of one transaction:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| funding | `92bb3f0e790ace19f1afec51141f87a3d6a911f10e82e765dba5368a6765667c` |
| spend | `fd0f553ee9a96b2cb48a4a9712824580910cd6056fc42f93f49eae83da2fb9e2` |
| input 0 | `pairing.publish`, 343,799 bytes |
| input 1 | `pairing.consume`, 475,017 bytes |
| the spend | 830,928 bytes, one OP_RETURN output |

The network verified that the Miller loop ran correctly on P and Q, that its
twelve outputs were published, that the same twelve were consumed, and that
their final exponentiation is e(P, Q).

What has **not** run on chain is a pairing in ONE SCRIPT. That is 817,031 bytes
against a 500,000-byte policy, and the 10,588 bytes by which the whole
exceeds its two stages are the plumbing the transaction replaced.

The last row carries its own caveat. `fp12.powX` — one f^|x| ladder,
uncompressed — was deployed and spent and is correct, and it is no longer what
the implementation does: `fp12.powXc` replaced it at 73,582 bytes. Counting
its bytes toward a pairing on chain would be counting a version that no longer
exists, so the figure above does not.

Compressed squaring is what made the second row possible: the final
exponentiation was 592,008 bytes before it and is 473,466 after, which is the
difference between over the policy boundary and under it.

## Table 8 — a Groth16 verifier across three inputs of one transaction

The three-pairing Miller loop alone is 705,838 bytes, past the policy, so
the loop itself is cut, at round 31 of 63. Built by `src/groth16spend.js` and every
input verified before these figures were taken.

| input | computes | locking | unlocking | of which subgroup checks |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | A, C ∈ G1; rounds 1–31 | 399,402 | 424,186 | 16,849 |
| 1 | rounds 32–63; B ∈ G2 | 371,834 | 383,299 | 957 |
| 2 | final exponentiation against e(α, β) | 475,647 | 481,527 | — |
| output | the blob, 44 field elements | 2,156 | — | — |

The transaction is 1,291,329 bytes. Its three OP_PUSH_TX preimages were ground
together over nLockTime, 168,127 tries for a triple. Every stage binds its
siblings through hashPrevouts, 56 bytes apiece.

**On mainnet**: funding `025f20f1d4156aa354afef37b1ec67e5c461f11375bc739902845a3b985dc5f0`, spend `cad6d2cca44fffb2f445009f392b668382d79d120b1c14db0fd4a8d192204bb6`. How the spend reached a block — refused by the relay path for its validation time, and taken directly by the pool that mined it — is §8.3.
